# 1. From Statistics to Machine Learning

---
name: stats_to_ml
description: Transition from statistical models to machine learning
# So far it was statistics, now it's ML

.center[<img src="assets/images/GraphML Class.png" alt="GraphML Class">]

---
# The "data model" tradition: building models from theory

<br>
### A lot of methods in this course come from the "data model" tradition:

<br>
- Understanding whether a network structure is random (CUG tests)

- Understanding what is the generative process (ERGM)

---
# Machine Learning is different

<br>
<br>
## ML is concerned with the other end

<br>
## It takes the network as a given, and sees how we can use it for different tasks

---
# You can do "naive" ML

<br>
### Use node features, centrality measures as inputs to ML models

<br>
### (In ML models you're allowed to use centrality as predictors, in regressions you're not)

<br>
### But... you're not really using the graph structure itself

---
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
# 2. Embeddings (the bread and butter)

---
# To "use" a graph for tasks you need embeddings

<br>
<br>
## To "use" a graph for tasks you need to turn it into a shape that algorithms can eat

<br>
## This shape is called: **EMBEDDINGS**

<br>
## This is going to be our bread and butter for today

---
# What is an embedding?

<br>
### Further reading for the curious: 
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLoROMvodv4rPLKxIpqhjhPgdQy7imNkDn

---
# Most ML tasks are inherently node-level

<br>
<br>
### Outcomes of people given their social graph, performance of firms given their allies, etc

<br>
### This is exactly what node-level tasks are about!

---
# Embeddings turn nodes into vectors

.center[<img src="assets/images/GraphML Class-1.png" alt="GraphML Class" style="width:70%">]

<br>
### Embeddings turn a node (or graph) into a vector

### Then we can feed this vector to any algorithm we like!

---
# The goal of embeddings

.center[<img src="assets/images/GraphML Class-2.png" alt="GraphML Class" style="width:70%">]

<br>
## Goal: similar position in the network = similar embedding vector

---
# Embeddings at a high level

<br>
### You need 3 things:

<br>
1. **Encoder**: looks up vector for any given node

2. **Decoder**: measures the similarity between two vectors

3. **Similarity definition**: what does "similar" mean? (distance in graph, topology, neighbors, etc.)

---
# The embedding framework

<br>
<br>
## Similarity(u,v) = Decoder( Encoder(u), Encoder(v) )

<br>
<br>
## Of these three components, we learn the encoder when training

---
# Different ways to make embeddings

<br>
## There are multiple approaches to creating embeddings

<br>
## Let's look at some key methods:
- Random walk
- DeepWalk
- Node2Vec

---
# Random walk embeddings

<br>
<br>
## Similarity(u,v) = P(u and v co-occur on a random walk over G)

<br>
<br>
### The similarity between two nodes is defined by how often they appear together on random walks through the graph

---
# DeepWalk

<br>
### Think word2vec, but for graphs!

<br>
- Walks are sentences
- Nodes are words
- Then we do skipgram next token prediction

<br>
### You just do a bunch of walks, that is your corpus

---
# Node2Vec

<br>
### Improved DeepWalk by adding biased walks

<br>
### Not every path has an equal probability

<br>
### You can tune how the walk-based exploration goes:
- BFS vs DFS
- Return parameter
- In-out parameter

---
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>
<br>

# 4. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs)

---

# Not every task needs the same information (embeddings)

<br>
<br>
## Different tasks require different kinds of information from a graph

<br>
## That's where GNNs come in

---
# Task-specific embeddings, end to end

<br>
## GNNs learn task-specific embeddings

<br>
## Different kinds of tasks:
- Node level (classification/regression)
- Edge level (link prediction)
- Graph level (graph classification)

---
# Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN)

<br>
## Key concepts:
- Compute graph
- Message passing
- Layers

---
# Compute Graphs in GCNs

.center[<img src="assets/images/GraphML Class-3.png" alt="GraphML Class" style="width:70%">]

## This graph determines how we aggregate information from neighbors

.footnote[From https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224w/slides/03-GNN1.pdf]

---
# Message passing

.center[<img src="assets/images/GraphML Class-4.png" alt="GraphML Class" style="width:70%">]

## You can just run backpropagation through all the aggregation neurons!

.footnote[From https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224w/slides/03-GNN1.pdf]


---
# GCN layers

.center[<img src="assets/images/GraphML Class-5.png" alt="GraphML Class" style="width:40%">]

### In GNNs we refer to degrees of separation as "hops"

2 layers = 2-hop aggregation for each node

## More layers = information from further away in the graph --> MORE ISN'T ALWAYS BETTER

.footnote[From https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224w/slides/03-GNN1.pdf]

---
# GCNs are generalized CNNs

<br>
<br>
## GCNs are basically more general CNNs

<br>
### In CNNs: neighborhood is defined by pixels (every node has 8 neighbors)

<br>
### In GCNs: neighborhood is defined by edges

---
# Graph Attention Networks (GAT)

<br>
<br>
<br>
## Not every neighbor is equally important

<br>
## Attention is all you need!

---
# And many more...

<br>
<br>
<br>
## There are many more GNN architectures

<br>
## But we don't have time to cover them all today
